paras: The harassment of Black pedestrians by white boys in Savannah was a series of incidents in which groups of white boys in parts of Savannah, Georgia, interfered with Black passersby, culminating on a Sunday afternoon in March 1903 when several women were "mistreated." The boys responsible were placed on a court docket and punished by their parents, and the Savannah Tribune warned that the practice could lead to "serious trouble."

According to the Savannah Tribune, "small white boys" commonly gathered in "certain sections of the city" and at times interfered with "colored persons in passing." The paper did not name the neighborhoods involved.

On a Sunday afternoon shortly before the Tribune's issue of March 28, 1903, probably March 22, several "ladies" were mistreated by such boys. The Tribune said the incident "nearly" turned into serious trouble but did not describe what the boys did, and it reported no injuries.

The boys found responsible "were docketed," and they were also punished by their parents. No report of a court hearing or penalty appears in the coverage, and the boys were not named. The Tribune urged that such boys be reported whenever they behaved improperly, arguing that otherwise they would "become bolder and commit offenses that may be more serious."

The only known account is a single paragraph in the editorial column of the Savannah Tribune, a Black weekly, on March 28, 1903. The Tribune called the boys a "lawless element" and placed the item among comments on Georgia's "separate car law" and on police officers it described as "adepts at using the club on the head of colored men" under arrest. No report of the incident was found in the white press, including Savannah's daily papers.

accounts.label: Savannah Tribune editorial column
accounts.gist: White boys gathering in parts of Savannah interfered with Black passersby; on a Sunday afternoon several ladies were mistreated, nearly causing serious trouble, and the guilty boys were docketed and punished by their parents.

framing.detail: The Tribune called the boys a 'lawless element', warned of 'serious trouble', and urged readers to report them, in a column that also criticized police clubbing of Black prisoners (A1).

quotes: In certain sections of the city small white boys generally gather and at times interfere with colored persons in passing.
This nearly happened on Sunday afternoon when several ladies were mistreated. The boys who were guilty were docketed. They were also punished by their parents.
This interference on the part of this lawless element may yet terminate into serious trouble.
